{{wiktionary|fifty-four}}
'''54''' ('''fifty-four''') is the [[natural number]] and [[Sign (math)|positive]] [[integer]] following [[53 (number)|53]] and preceding [[55 (number)|55]]. As a multiple of [[2]] but not of [[4]], 54 is an [[Singly and doubly even|oddly]] [[even number]] and a [[composite number]].

54 is related to the [[golden ratio]] through [[trigonometry]]: the [[sine]] of a 54 degree angle is half of the golden ratio. Also, 54 is a [[regular number]], and its even division of powers of 60 was useful to ancient mathematicians who used the [[Assyro-Babylonian mathematics]] system.

==In mathematics==
===Number theory===
[[File:Square-sum-54.png|thumb|54 as the sum of three positive squares|alt=Three stacks of 54 cubes. Each stack is composed of three tiers. Each tier contains a number of cubes arranged in a square.]]
54 is an [[abundant number]]<ref name="abundant">{{Cite OEIS|A005101|name=Abundant numbers (sum of divisors of m exceeds 2m)}}</ref> because [[Aliquot sum|the sum of its proper divisors]] ([[66 (number)|66]]),<ref name="aliquot">{{Cite OEIS|A001065|name=Sum of proper divisors (or aliquot parts) of n: sum of divisors of n that are less than n.}}</ref> is greater than itself. Like all multiples of [[6]],<ref>{{cite journal | zbl=0266.10012 | mr=360455 | last1=Zachariou | first1=Andreas | last2=Zachariou | first2=Eleni | title=Perfect, Semiperfect and Ore Numbers | journal=Bull. Soc. Math. Grèce |series=Nouvelle Série | volume=13 | pages=12–22 | year=1972 }}</ref> 54 is equal to some of its proper divisors summed together,{{efn|text=54 can be expressed as: {{nowrap|9 + 18 + 27}} = 54.}} so it is also a [[semiperfect number]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A005835| Pseudoperfect (or semiperfect) numbers}}</ref> These proper divisors can be summed in various ways to express all positive integers smaller than 54, so 54 is a [[practical number]] as well.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A005153|name=Practical numbers: positive integers m such that every k <= sigma(m) is a sum of distinct divisors of m. Also called panarithmic numbers.}}</ref> Additionally, as an integer for which the [[arithmetic mean]] of all its [[Sign (mathematics)|positive]] [[divisor]]s (including itself) is also an integer, 54 is an [[arithmetic number]].<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A003601|name=Numbers j such that the average of the divisors of j is an integer: sigma_0(j) divides sigma_1(j). Alternatively, numbers j such that tau(j) (A000005(j)) divides sigma(j) (A000203(j)).}}</ref>

===Trigonometry and the golden ratio===
If the [[complementary angle]] of a triangle's corner is 54 [[Degree (angle)|degrees]], the [[sine]] of that angle is half the [[golden ratio]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Khan |first=Sameen Ahmed |date=2020-10-11 |title=Trigonometric Ratios Using Geometric Methods |url=https://www.research-publication.com/amsj/all-issues/vol-09/iss-10 |journal=Advances in Mathematics: Scientific Journal |language=en |volume=9 |issue=10 |pages=8698 |doi=10.37418/amsj.9.10.94 |issn=1857-8365|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite OEIS|A019863|name=Decimal expansion of sin(3*Pi/10) (sine of 54 degrees, or cosine of 36 degrees).}}</ref> This is because the corresponding interior angle is equal to [[Pi|{{pi}}]]/5 [[radian]]s (or [[36 (number)|36]] degrees).{{efn|text=There are various ways to prove this, but the algebraic method will eventually show that <math display=inline>\sin{54} = \cos{\frac{\pi}{5}} = \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{4} = \frac{\phi}{2}</math>.}} If that triangle is [[isoceles triangle|isoceles]], the relationship with the golden ratio makes it a [[Golden triangle (mathematics)|golden triangle]]. The golden triangle is most readily found as the spikes on a regular [[pentagram]].

===Regular number used in Assyro-Babylonian mathematics===
As a [[regular number]], 54 is a divisor of many powers of 60.{{efn|text=60{{sup|3}} and its multiples are divisible by 54.}} This is an important property in [[Assyro-Babylonian mathematics]] because that system uses a [[sexagesimal]] (base-60) number system. In base 60, the [[Multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of a regular number has a finite representation. Babylonian [[Computer (occupation)|computers]] kept tables of these reciprocals to make their work more efficient. Using regular numbers simplifies multiplication and division in base 60 because dividing {{mvar|a}} by {{mvar|b}} can be done by multiplying {{mvar|a}} by {{mvar|b}}'s reciprocal when {{mvar|b}} is a regular number.<ref>{{citation | author-link = Aaboe | last = Aaboe | first = Asger | title = Some Seleucid mathematical tables (extended reciprocals and squares of regular numbers) | journal = [[Journal of Cuneiform Studies]] | volume = 19 | issue = 3 | pages = 79–86 | year = 1965 | mr = 0191779 | doi = 10.2307/1359089 | publisher = The American Schools of Oriental Research | jstor = 1359089| s2cid = 164195082 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation| last = Sachs | first = A. J. | year = 1947 | title = Babylonian mathematical texts. I. Reciprocals of regular sexagesimal numbers | journal = [[Journal of Cuneiform Studies]] | volume = 1 | issue = 3 | pages = 219–240 | mr = 0022180  | doi = 10.2307/1359434 | publisher = The American Schools of Oriental Research | jstor = 1359434| s2cid = 163783242}}</ref>

For instance, division by 54 can be achieved in the Assyro-Babylonian system by multiplying by [[4000 (number)|4000]] because {{nowrap|60{{sup|3}} ÷ 54}} = {{nowrap|60{{sup|3}} × (1/54)}} = 4000. In base 60, 4000 can be written as 1:6:40.{{efn|text=1:6:40 = {{nowrap|1×60{{sup|2}} + 6×60{{sup|1}} + 40×60{{sup|0}}}} = 4000. This is the number written in Babylonian numerals: 𒐕𒐚𒐏.}} Because the Assyro-Babylonian system does not have a [[Decimal point|symbol]] separating the [[fraction]]al and integer parts of a number<ref name="BabFrac">{{Cite journal |last=Cajori |first=Florian |date=1922 |title=Sexagesimal Fractions Among the Babylonians |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2972914 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=8–10 |doi=10.2307/2972914 |jstor=2972914 |issn=0002-9890}}</ref> and [[Babylonian cuneiform numerals#Zero|does not have the concept]] of [[0]] as a number,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |date=1944 |title=Zero: The Symbol, the Concept, the Number |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3030083 |journal=National Mathematics Magazine |volume=18 |issue=8 |pages=323–330 |doi=10.2307/3030083 |jstor=3030083 |issn=1539-5588|url-access=subscription }}</ref> it does not specify the power of the starting digit. Accordingly, 1/54 can also be written as 1:6:40.{{efn|text=1:6:40 = 1×60{{sup|-1}} + 6×60{{sup|-2}} + 40×60{{sup|-3}} = 1/54. This is the number written in Babylonian numerals: 𒐕𒐚𒐏.}}<ref name="BabFrac"/> Therefore, the result of multiplication by 1:6:40 (4000) has the same Assyro-Babylonian representation as the result of multiplication by 1:6:40 (1/54). To convert from the former to the latter, the result's representation is interpreted as a number shifted three base-60 places to the right, reducing it by a factor of 60{{sup|3}}.{{efn|text=For example, {{nowrap|6534 ÷ 54}} = 121. The Assyro-Babylonian method is to calculate {{nowrap|6534 × 4000}} = 26136000. This result can be written in Babylonian numerals as 𒐖𒐕 (2:1), meaning {{nowrap|2×60{{sup|4}} + 1×60{{sup|3}}}}. To complete the division by 54, one must divide by 60{{sup|3}}. Shifting the numeral three base-60 digits to the right divides the number by 60{{sup|3}}, so 𒐖𒐕 (2:1) is already the answer: {{nowrap|2×60{{sup|1}} + 1×60{{sup|0}}}} = 121.}}

===Graph theory===
[[File:Ellingham-Horton 54-graph.svg|thumb|The Ellingham–Horton 54-graph]]
The second [[Ellingham–Horton graph]] was published by [[Mark Ellingham|Mark N. Ellingham]] and Joseph D. Horton in 1983; it is of order 54.<ref>{{citation|last1=Ellingham|first1=M. N.|last2=Horton|first2=J. D.|title=Non-Hamiltonian 3-connected cubic bipartite graphs|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B|volume=34|issue=3|doi=10.1016/0095-8956(83)90046-1|pages=350–353|year=1983|doi-access=free}}.</ref> These [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] provided further counterexamples to the conjecture of [[W. T. Tutte]] that every [[cubic graph|cubic]] 3-connected [[bipartite graph]] is [[Hamiltonian graph|Hamiltonian]].<ref>{{citation|last=Tutte|first=W. T.|title=On the 2-factors of bicubic graphs|journal=Discrete Mathematics|volume=1|issue=2|pages=203–208|year=1971|doi=10.1016/0012-365X(71)90027-6|doi-access=free}}.</ref> Horton disproved the conjecture some years earlier with the [[Horton graph]], but that was larger at 92 vertices.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/HortonGraphs.html |title=Horton Graphs |access-date=2025-04-11 }}</ref> The smallest known counter-example is now 50 vertices.<ref>{{citation|last=Georges|first=J. P.|title=Non-hamiltonian bicubic graphs|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B|volume=46|issue=1|doi=10.1016/0095-8956(89)90012-9|pages=121–124|year=1989|doi-access=}}.</ref>

==In literature==
In ''[[The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy]]'' by [[Douglas Adams]], the "[[Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything]]" famously was [[42 (number)|42]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Adams |first=Douglas |title=The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy |title-link=The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (novel) |year=1979 |page=179-80}}</ref> Eventually, one character's unsuccessful attempt to divine the Ultimate Question elicited "What do you get if you multiply six by nine?"<ref name="Restaurant">{{Cite book |last=Adams |first=Douglas |title=The Restaurant at the End of the Universe |title-link=The Restaurant at the End of the Universe |year=1980 |page=181-84}}</ref> The mathematical answer was 54, not 42. Some readers who were trying to find a deeper meaning in the passage soon noticed the fact was true in [[base 13]]: the base-10 expression 54{{sub|10}} can be encoded as the base-13 expression {{nowrap|6{{sub|13}} × 9{{sub|13}}}} = 42{{sub|13}}.<ref name="scripts">{{Cite book |last=Adams |first=Douglas |author-link=Douglas Adams |title=The Original Hitchhiker Radio Scripts |title-link=The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy: The Original Radio Scripts |date=1985 |publisher=Pan Books |isbn=0-330-29288-9 |editor-last=Perkins |editor-first=Geoffrey |editor-link=Geoffrey Perkins |location=London |pages=128}}</ref> Adams said this was a coincidence.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://io9.gizmodo.com/5659984/today-is-the-ultimate-answer-to-the-ultimate-question-of-life-the-universe-and-everything |title=Today Is 101010: The Ultimate Answer to the Ultimate Question |last=Diaz |first=Jesus |website=[[io9]] |access-date=8 May 2017 |language=en-US |archive-date=26 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170526041851/https://io9.gizmodo.com/5659984/today-is-the-ultimate-answer-to-the-ultimate-question-of-life-the-universe-and-everything |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Explanatory footnotes==
[[File:Genji_chapter_symbols_groupings_of_5_elements.svg|thumb|''Genji-mon'', the traditional symbols that represent the fifty-four chapters of ''[[The Tale of Genji]]''|alt=These symbols are abstract geometry that does not directly map onto the numbers' values. The core feature is that they all involve at least five vertical parallel lines. For example, 2 is just five vertical parallel lines that do not touch. 53 is those five lines connected at the top. 54 is all of the lines connected, alternating top and bottom, so it looks like a winding snake.]]
